caption:
How were the pyramids built? The honest answer: nobody has the method written down.

The Great Pyramid was built around 2600 BC for the pharaoh Khufu, in roughly 26 years. It took an estimated 2.3 million blocks — about 5.5 million tonnes of limestone, 8,000 tonnes of granite, and 500,000 tonnes of mortar. Many alternative and contradictory theories exist for the exact construction techniques. There is no definite consensus.

What there is, is evidence. Fires used in mixing the mortar left charcoal in it; 46 samples taken in 1984 and 1995 radiocarbon dated to 2871–2604 BC. In 1837 tunnellers broke into four sealed chambers above the King's Chamber and found the walls covered in red paint — work-gang graffiti naming Khufu over a dozen times, e.g. "The gang, The white crown of Khnum-Khufu is powerful."

Worker graffiti at Giza shows haulers organised in groups of 40, each with four sub-units under an "Overseer of Ten". A 1999 management study estimated an average workforce of 13,200, peaking near 40,000. In a modern experiment, four workers cut a 2.5-tonne block in 4 days using replica arsenic-copper chisels and wooden mallets — six times faster once the stone was wetted.

Still open: in 2017 muon radiography found a cavity at least 30 metres long above the Grand Gallery. Its purpose is unknown and it cannot be reached. The shafts off the Queen's Chamber end in limestone "doors"; nobody knows what they are for.

Images: Gary Todd, 2002; Warren LeMay, 2019; mortar specimen, reign of Khufu, Metropolitan Museum; Perring, 1839; Luigi Mayer, c. 1800; Selim Hassan, 1936.
